Ask about King Menkaure, his pyramid complex, or the services at this station.

Pyramid of King Menkaure is the smallest of the three Kings’ pyramids with current height of 61 meters, built for Menkaure, grandson of Khufu between 2532–2503 BC.

It’s known for its granite casing on the lower quarter.

Its granite massive blocks were quarried in city of Aswan, which is over 800 km away, and were transported from there.

Rest of the building is made with limestones.

Around the King Menkaure Pyramid you will see the three smaller Queens’ Pyramids which were built for the Queens of his age.

It’s believed that the biggest of them was for his Queen.

You will also see next to it (on the eastern face of the King Menkaure’s Pyramid) the Funerary Temple of Menkaure, which was built from mud bricks.

Despite the weak capabilities to build the Funerary Temple of Menkaure, the mortuary rituals were made to sustain the King’s spirit for 300 years after his burial.
Ask about King Menkaure, his pyramid, the Queens’ Pyramids, or the Funerary Temple.

Ask about King Khafre, his pyramid complex, station services, or the plateau map.

Pyramid of King Khafre is the second-tallest pyramid, built between 2558–2532 BC, its height is 143.5 meters.

Its peak still preserves the beautifully polished blocks of high-quality white limestone that once encased the majority of the structure.

The white limestones were quarried in city of Turah, south of Maadi city, and were transported by ships.

Next to it you will find the Mortuary Temple of Khafre: Unlike earlier structures, which is among the best preserved of the old kingdom.

It was connected by a sloping causeway to the highly preserved Valley Temple of Khafre, which is on the east side of the Khafre Pyramid.

The Valley Temple is made of massive limestone blocks encased in granite, the floors are made of alabaster, and its wide hall features monolithic granite pillars.

The hall of the valley temple once accommodated the statues of King Khafre, one of these is the famous granodiorite statue of Khafre with Horus as a falcon perched behind his head, which is considered one of the masterpieces of ancient Egyptian art.

The complex is closely connected to the Great Sphinx, which is conveniently positioned beside the valley temple.

There is much more to tell you about this complex.

Enjoy!
Ask about King Khafre, his pyramid, the mortuary and valley temples, or the Great Sphinx.

East of Khafre Pyramid you will find Khentkawes Monument, which is the two stepped tomb built for Queen Mother Khentkawes of the fourth dynasty.

West of Khafre Pyramid you will find the remains of the big Workers’ Town and Cemetery, which is called Heit al-Ghurab (Arabic for “Wall of the Crow”).

This is where the workers who built the pyramid complexes of Khafre (between 2558–2532 BC) and Menkaure (between 2532–2503 BC) lived.

The tantalizing remains of an even older settlement underneath may date back to King Khufu’s reign (c.2589–2566 BC). Houses, warehouses, three main streets, and a royal administrative building were discovered within the city walls, as were four huge galleries.

These may have been the barracks in which the workers who built the pyramids slept and prepared their food.

An enormous amount of fish, bird, cattle, sheep, goat, and pig bones were found, revealing that the state ensured that the workers were in good health so they could fulfill their physically demanding responsibilities.
Ask about the Khentkawes Monument, Heit al-Ghurab, the workers’ cemetery, or the settlement discoveries.

On the foot of the hill, immediately to the west of Heit al-Ghurab is the town’s cemetery.

Low-ranking overseers of workmen were buried in modest mastabas (Arabic for “benches”) on the low slopes of the hill’s foot, surrounded by smaller mastabas or domed graves, possibly for their extended families or the workers they supervised.

These were largely built of mudbrick.

Whereas the higher-ranking overseers and skilled craftsmen were buried in large stone mastabas higher up the slope.

Among these is the beautifully decorated tomb of the overseer of linen manufacturing also the overseer of royal authority of purification, Nefertheith.

The majority of the discovered human remains show evidence of hard physical labor, many of them featuring broken bones.

Most of them had healed correctly, which indicates they received very good medical care along with sound nutrition for the treatment.

When you’re done navigating this beautiful place, click next for the next station, station 5.

Head north to see the Great Sphinx of Giza, which is one of the most famous hallmarks of the ancient Egyptian civilization.

It was carved directly out of bedrock during the 4th Dynasty (between 2613–2494 BC), it’s the oldest colossal statue. It’s 73 meters long and 20 meters high.

Ancient Egyptian sphinxes represented the king with the body of a lion, in a clear demonstration of his power.

The Great Sphinx was carved during the reign of King Khafre.

The Great Sphinx’s facial analysis has revealed striking similarities with those of Khafre’s statues.

You will walk through the Sphinx Temple to enjoy the architecture of the temple and get a close-up view of the Sphinx at the end of the ascending isle on the second right after you enter.

The Great Pyramid of King Khufu

Infront of you will see the Great King Khufu Pyramid: the oldest and largest of the three main pyramids, built between 2589–2566 BC.

Its height is 146.5 meters and was the tallest structure in the world for 3800 years.

It took an estimate of 10 to 20 years to build.

The Khufu Pyramid was made of local use limestone, and its exterior was once entirely covered with high quality polished white limestone.

These casing stones were brought from City of Turah, south of Maadi City, by ship.

On the inside, the pyramid has three burial chambers, one is carved into the bedrock, and two built on height within the masonry itself, which is an interior structure that no other pyramid possesses.

You can see the sarcophagus in which King Khufu was once laid to rest in the high chamber (The King’s Chamber).

You can access the chamber through a passage that has a great of size corbelled ascending ceiling, which is masterpiece of ancient architecture.

Two large dismantled ships were discovered in pits in the south side of the pyramid.

We believe the ships were used to transport the King’s Mummy and Funerary Furniture to the Pyramid.

Adjacent to King Khufu’s Pyramid there are 3 smaller Queens’ Pyramids.

On the east side of King Khufu Pyramid you will see King Khufu’s Funerary Temple.
Ask about King Khufu, the Great Pyramid, its chambers, casing stones, or the two ships.

You will also see the Tomb of Queen Meresankh III, who is the wife of Khafre and granddaughter of Khufu.

The Tomb of Queen is very large and exquisitely decorated, made worthy of her rank and fortunately also contains one of the best preserved wall reliefs.

The walls are decorated with a diverse array of scenes, including bread baking, beer brewing, fowling, herding, mat making, metal smelting, and the sculpting of statues, apparently of Meresankh herself.

There are also elaborate scenes of offering-bearers bringing all sorts of gifts to Meresankh, which is intended to provide her soul with a continuous stream of food and goods in her afterlife.

Among the objects that are brought to her is a canopy with a bed being set up within it, an armchair, and a carrying chair. Similar objects to those were discovered in the tomb of Hetepheres I, the mother of Khufu, and can be seen today at the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

Among the most striking features of Meresankh’s tomb chapel is a series of ten large statues of women that are carved out of the northern wall.

It is believed that they represent, in addition to Meresankh herself, her mother, and daughters as well.
Ask about Queen Meresankh III, her decorated tomb chapel, its wall scenes, or the ten statues.

You will also see on the east and west sides of the King Khufu Pyramid the Eastern and Western Cemeteries, which are two of the largest preserved Old Kingdom cemeteries.

They include the tombs of members of the royal family and the highest-ranking nobles.

As such, they contain some of the most beautiful tomb decorations from this period.

The cemeteries consist mostly mastabas (Arabic for “benches”), in addition to rock-cut tombs. It’s a funerary structure that is rectangular in shape and built over the tomb proper, which is positioned underground.

Most of the mastabas of the Eastern and Western Cemeteries were built during the reign of Khufu, in tandem with his pyramid complex, whereas the rock-cut tombs were built later.

Most of the tombs of the Eastern Cemetery dating to the reign of Khufu were intended for his closest relatives.

The rock-cut tomb of his mother, queen Hetepheres I, along with her funerary equipment, were discovered around the site of the mastaba of his half-brother Ankh-haf, who had an important administrative position in the construction of the Great Pyramid.

On the other hand, the mastabas of the Western Cemetery, which are mostly arranged in an orderly grid, were reserved for very high-ranking noblemen that were not as closely related to the king.

Among of which is the monumental mastaba of Hemiunu, who oversaw the building of the Great Pyramid.
